title: The Single Word “Knowing”
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Question: Does the fundamental mind (the true mind) know, or does it not know?

inline.s: Question: Does the fundamental mind (the true mind) know, or does it not know?
[Fundamental mind] See in detail
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathāgatagarbha
Answer: It knows. The Śūraṅgama Sutra says:
“When knowing and seeing establish knowledge, that is the root of ignorance.”

This shows that before ignorance arises there is originally knowledge, and this is the knowledge of the fundamental mind. This knowledge is the knowledge of prajñā. But the knowledge that is established is the knowledge of the cognitive mind’s seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing — namely, the conditioned shadows of the six sense-objects.
The Śūraṅgama Sutra then goes on to say:
“When knowing and seeing are without seeing, this is nirvāṇa.”
This knowledge without seeing is the knowledge of the fundamental mind.
In his Notes on the Lankāvatāra, Master Hanshan says:
“When the mind is quiescent and knows, leaving both true and false behind, this is called self-awakened sage wisdom.”
In his Chan School’s Yongjia Collection
Fourth, “Ode on Śamatha,” Master Yongjia says:
“After conditions are forgotten, all is still and silent, while the nature of spiritual knowing
(the mind-essence)
shines clear and distinct.”
Sengzhao’s Treatise on the Unknowing of Prajñā says:

“Because the sage’s mind does not know, it knows everything. The knowledge that does not know is called all-knowledge. Therefore a sutra says: ‘The sage’s mind knows nothing, and knows everything.’ How true this is!”
Question: The single word “knowing” has long been a matter of debate. Master Guifeng said:
“The one word ‘knowing’ is the gate of all wonders.”
Chan Master Huanglong Sixin said:
“The one word ‘knowing’ is the gate of all misfortunes.”
May I ask, which is right?
Answer: The Śūraṅgama Sutra says:
“When knowing and seeing establish knowledge, that is the root of ignorance.”

The first “knowing” in this sentence is the gate of all wonders; but if one sinks into the second “knowing,” that is a diseased eye seeing flowers in the sky, and going further to invite those sky-flowers to bear sky-fruit — this is the gate of all misfortunes. Master Hanshan said:

“Before the Buddha appeared in the world, before the Patriarch came from the West, the ready-made household estate was already complete in every person. Because they had it completely yet did not know it, the Yellow-Faced One
(Śākyamuni Buddha)
and the Blue-Eyed One
(Patriarch Bodhidharma)
could not help themselves, and deliberately came forth to explain it clearly for people. The millions of the assembly on Vulture Peak, and the seventeen hundred
(the seventeen hundred koans in the Transmission of the Lamp and the like)

, were all called back with a single call, and suddenly knew what they had originally possessed. This is ‘the one word knowing is the gate of all wonders.’ Alas! The Buddha and the Patriarchs never had any real dharma to give people; who would have expected that everyone’s diseased eye would see flowers in the sky, and that they would further invite those flowers to bear fruit — could this have been the Buddha’s and Patriarchs’ intention? This is ‘the one word knowing is the gate of all misfortunes.’ If we do not again scrape with the golden lancet
(to remove the film from the eye, lest the diseased eye see flowers in the sky)
, how shall we
(inherit, take up)
this household estate?”
(Dream Journey Collection
Preface to Sending Master Wuyan Dao to Serve as Abbot of Shaolin) The Elder Zibai said:
“The one word knowing is the gate of all wonders; to establish knowledge upon knowing-and-seeing — how great the misfortune!”
(Collection of the Elder Zibai)
[The one word knowing is the gate of all wonders]
Guifeng
Master, in his Preface to the Collected Writings on the Source of Chan, says:

All dharmas are like dreams, as all the sages alike proclaim. Therefore deluded thoughts are fundamentally still, and sense-objects are fundamentally empty. The empty, still mind, with its spiritual knowing undimmed

This very knowing of the empty and still is your true nature. Whether deluded or awakened, the mind in itself knows, without depending on conditions to arise, without arising from objects. The one word knowing is the gate of all wonders. Because from time without beginning we have been deluded, we falsely cling to body and mind as a self, and give rise to thoughts of greed, anger, and the like. If we obtain the guidance of a good friend and suddenly awaken to the knowing of the empty and still

Since this knowing has no thought and no form, where is the mark of self or the mark of person? Awaken to the emptiness of all marks, and the mind is naturally without thought. When a thought arises, immediately awaken; the moment it is awakened it is gone

— the wondrous gate of cultivation lies precisely here. Therefore, though one cultivates the myriad practices in full, one takes no-thought as the sole principle. Once one attains the knowledge and view of no-thought, love and hate naturally grow faint, compassion and wisdom naturally increase in brightness, sins and karma are naturally cut off, and merit and practice naturally advance. Once one has understood that all marks are no-marks, there is naturally the cultivation of no-cultivation. When afflictions are exhausted, birth and death come to an end
When arising and ceasing have ceased, still illumination appears before one, its functioning inexhaustible — and this is named Buddha.
Therefore, “the one word knowing is the gate of all wonders” means: the knowing of the empty and still is the gate of all wonders.

[The knowing of the empty and still] The knowing of the empty and still is the knowing of no-thought; to distinguish it from the mark-grasping knowing of seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing, it is also called “spiritual knowing.” (See in detail
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathāgatagarbha
.) The Śūraṅgama Sutra says:

“When knowing and seeing establish knowledge, that is the root of ignorance; when knowing and seeing are without seeing, this is nirvāṇa, the true purity beyond outflow.” In his Notes on the Lankāvatāra, Master Hanshan says: “When the mind is quiescent and knows, leaving both true and false behind, this is called self-awakened sage wisdom.”

[Could not help themselves] could not suppress a smile. “Rěnjùn” means to hold back a smile; “bùjīn” means unable to control oneself. [Scrape again with the golden lancet] to remove the film from the eye, lest the diseased eye see flowers in the sky. A poem says: “The tangled films on the eye are scraped away with the golden lancet.” [Golden lancet] an ancient tool for treating eye disease, shaped like an arrowhead and used to scrape the film from the eye.
Conclusion: The knowing of the empty and still is the gate of all wonders. The knowing of discrimination is the gate of all misfortunes.
